newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: US growth embarasses Europe to prod economies.
newsitem.headline: US growth embarasses Europe to prod economies.

text.p: European corporate and government leaders, embarrassed by the latest confirmation of solid U.S. growth, are saying they have to redouble efforts to revive their weak economies.

As Clinton administration officials crowed over U.S. performance at the annual World Economic Forum, many Europeans with them in this Alpine resort said at the weekend they were paying more attention to the U.S. model of low taxes, little social welfare and unfettered competition.

"This doesn't mean that we have to replicate in Europe exactly what they have done in the United States. But we have to look around and see how other countries are more successful in fighting unemployment," Belgian Finance Minister Philippe Maystadt told Reuters.
"I think this implies that we go further in reforms in the goods and services markets and in the labour markets," Maystadt said.

Labour rules limiting such things as weekend and night work or part-time contracts are a particular focus of attention by European governments including the German and French, but moves to loosen them have been slowed by union and public protests.
Britain is something of an exception, with forecasts its growth will lead the continental economies this year due in part to a greater degree of deregulation.

Maystadt said the United States was in "an ideal situation" after fourth-quarter 1996 data on Friday confirmed nearly six years of gross domestic product (GDP) growth and the lowest inflation in 30 years.
Louis Schweitzer, chairman and chief executive of French carmaker Renault, said the United States was drawing increasing interest from continental European policy makers.
"The U.S. is showing that you can have sustained, non-inflationary growth and this is good," Schweitzer said.

While European inflation is under control, European Commission figures show the European Union has managed to create only 10 million new jobs since the 1960s, less than one fifth of what the United States has achieved.

EU unemployment now stands at 11 percent compared with about 5.5 percent in the United States and the EU level of gross domestic product (GDP) per capita is nearly one third below that of the United States.

"It is an embarassment," said Georges Ugeux, New York Stock Exchange executive vice president in charge of international business and a Belgian national who formerly worked as a fund manager for the European Union.
"It is more than an embarassment in the sense that it is painful, because at the end of the day the issue is that we should have more people having jobs, we should have higher growth," he said.
Even Jacques Santer, president of the European Commission and a staunch defender of its performance, acknowledged there was a widespread perception the EU was uncompetitive and economically weak.

"Nowadays, Europe is too often in the dock as the accused," he said, then argued the facts showed Europe was strong and moving firmly towards a common currency that would help boost growth by making the bloc more competitive.
"Europe continues to be a social, economic and political model for many parts of the world," Santer told a Davos panel discussion on Europe's future.
Ironically, one of the strongest warnings against the U.S. economic formula came at Davos from an American, president John Sweeny of the labour federation AFL/CIO.
Sweeney said U.S. growth was built on the back of underemployment and weak social benefits that go against the grain of continental Europe's well-organised workers.

"Far from being a cure-all, the attempt of any advanced European social democracy to imbibe the neo-liberal version of the U.S. model would create massive social upheaval, with far greater economic costs than benefits," Sweeney said.
